Transcript:
[00:00] Maria Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Maria, AE for Voltix, and Arjun is gonna run the bench for us.
[00:12] Lena Ortiz: Hi, thanks. We really wanna make sure the POC shows not just functional parity but predictable economics and latency under load.
[00:21] Arjun Patel: Totally, yep. Today's agenda is to lock pass/fail thresholds and the reporting packet so the team can sign off after the runs. We'll go through workload mix, metrics, and what artifacts you'll get.
[00:34] Samir Khan: For context, our production pattern is spiky — lots of short chat messages and periodic long summarizations. We'll upload a 10k prompt set that mirrors that mix.
[00:44] Priya Desai: And product-wise we need to know when to degrade to cheaper models; acceptable user-facing latency is a big factor.
[00:52] Maria Chen: Great. Let's propose concrete thresholds and then you tell us if they match your bar. Arjun?
[00:57] Arjun Patel: OK. For latency, propose P50 < 120ms for short chat prompts (<= 128 tokens), P95 < 350ms, P99 < 900ms. For long-form summarization (>= 1024 tokens) P95 < 2s, P99 < 4s. Throughput target is sustaining 200 requests/minute in dedicated pilot mode without queue growth.
[01:24] Lena Ortiz: P95 at 350ms seems a touch high for our interactive product — we were hoping for ~200–250ms. Is that realistic at our scale?
[01:31] Arjun Patel: We can tighten to P95 < 250ms for the short-chat path if you commit to dedicated pool sizing we recommend (2x A100-equivalent for baseline), and if you accept aggressive batching tuned for peak windows. But that will have cost implications.
[01:46] Samir Khan: Ok, cost ballpark? We need $/1M tokens to be under $15 for total infra+plat during pilot.
[01:54] Maria Chen: Historically for similar mixes on Redwood Dedicated the working number is $9–13 per 1M effective tokens with quantization + KV caching. We'll produce a cost projection in the results packet.
[02:05] Priya Desai: On quality, our ML team will provide a golden-labeled subset (2k examples). We need pass criteria: no more than 2% drop in task-level F1 relative to our on-prem baseline, and hallucination incidents under 1% of sampled outputs.
[02:20] Arjun Patel: That matches what we've seen — we'll compute per-run regression vs your baseline and flag any samples with hallucination heuristics.
[02:27] Lena Ortiz: How do you define hallucination in the report? We need reproducible rules.
[02:31] Arjun Patel: We'll surface a flagged list of outputs where the model asserts unverifiable facts or contradicts the source. That'll be a CSV column 'hallucination_flag' with notes. We'll also include a sample size and manual check notes.
[02:43] Samir Khan: For acceptance, is the rule absolute or graded? For example, if latency is 10% over threshold but quality is better, can we still pass?
[02:51] Maria Chen: Good question. We suggest a weighted pass/fail rubric: must pass all hard gates (no critical security/SSO/KMS failures, and hallucination below ceiling). For soft gates like latency/cost/throughput, use a scoring where 80+% total score passes. We'll share a one-pager rubric.
[03:07] Priya Desai: Please make that rubric explicit. Product needs clear go/no-go language for stakeholders.
[03:12] Arjun Patel: We'll include a PASS/FAIL per-metric and an overall verdict. Example: Hard gates: Security (SOC2 evidence + SAML/SCIM), Data isolation verified — must be green. Performance gates: each gets points; we compute weighted average.
[03:25] Lena Ortiz: Fine. Walk me through the acceptance test run itself.
[03:28] Arjun Patel: We'll run a 48-hour soak with your 10k prompt set in a loop. The workload mix we agreed: 60% short chat (<128 tokens), 30% embeddings/inference for similarity (we'll include embedding-perf), 10% long form. We'll measure per-request latency, CPU/GPU utilization, token-level cost, and steady-state throughput.
[03:46] Samir Khan: Will you run on Hosted or Dedicated for this POC? We prefer Dedicated to mirror production.
[03:50] Maria Chen: We're proposing Redwood Dedicated for the pilot (predictable throughput and isolation). We'll still include a Hosted fallback run to show different economics.
[03:58] Arjun Patel: And we will do two phases: Phase A — baseline single-node run to validate correctness. Phase B — scaled run (2x nodes) to show linearity.
[04:07] Lena Ortiz: Sounds good. What about observability artifacts?
[04:10] Arjun Patel: Deliverables: 1) Executive summary PDF (1–2 pages) with verdict, key numbers, and recommendations. 2) Raw CSV per-request (timestamp, route, prompt_id, tokens_in, tokens_out, latency_ms, model_variant, cost_estimate, hallucination_flag). 3) Jupyter notebook with charts and reproducible analysis. 4) Deployment config used for bench (YAML) and a small runbook. We'll put everything in a shared S3/Drive folder link.
[04:33] Priya Desai: We need the executive summary to include the exact rubric and a short table we can paste into the steering deck.
[04:38] Maria Chen: We'll include a one-slide table and a one-slide risk/mitigation section.
[04:41] Samir Khan: On telemetry — we'll want request-level traces for ~1% of requests to debug outliers. Is that feasible?
[04:47] Arjun Patel: Yep, we can enable tracing and attach sample traces; they will be redacted per your privacy rules. We'll need your S3 pointer and a short-lived token to push logs.
[04:55] Lena Ortiz: Security — quick check. We require KMS integration, SSO, and audit logs. Do you have a SOC2 report?
[05:01] Maria Chen: Yes. I'll send the SOC2 report and our security whitepaper. For KMS we support customer-managed keys for Private and Dedicated. For Hosted we support bring-your-own-key via our KMS integration.
[05:11] Priya Desai: Great. Add that to the packet.
[05:13] Samir Khan: Test schedule — when can we start? We have the prompt set ready, but need the S3 creds.
[05:18] Maria Chen: If Samir uploads the prompt set and grants Arjun read access by end of day Wednesday (2025-12-17), we can schedule the bench to start 2025-12-18 and finish 2025-12-20, and deliver artifacts by 2025-12-22.
[05:30] Lena Ortiz: That timeline works.
[05:33] Arjun Patel: Regarding reporting format details — CSV column names will be: run_id, timestamp_utc, prompt_id, route, model, tokens_in, tokens_out, latency_ms, cpu_pct, gpu_mem_mb, cost_usd_est, hallucination_flag, notes. We'll include a checksum/hash of the prompt set used.
[05:51] Samir Khan: Good. Also ask that any prompt preprocessing is documented (trimming, tokenization) so metrics align.
[05:57] Arjun Patel: We'll surface the exact tokenizer version and any prompt truncation rules in the runbook.
[06:04] Priya Desai: Acceptance example: If P95 is 260ms (target 250ms), and weighted score becomes 77%, is that a fail? We need a tolerance band.
[06:13] Maria Chen: We'll include a tolerance band: within 10% of target reduces points by 50% for that metric; beyond 10% is a hard fail only if combined with other metric misses that exceed threshold. But again, hallucination and security are hard gates.
[06:27] Lena Ortiz: Makes sense. Please make the math explicit in the rubric.
[06:31] Arjun Patel: We'll add the scoring formula and an example calculation in the notebook and PDF.
[06:36] Samir Khan: One more — regression detection. If model output quality drops on certain buckets, do you support per-bucket aborts?
[06:43] Arjun Patel: We do. We will break down metrics by bucket (intent type, prompt length, domain) and if a critical bucket has >3% absolute drop in F1, we flag it as a blocker for that bucket and include mitigation steps.
[06:55] Maria Chen: Ok let's capture next steps — (reads) Arjun runs bench, Samir uploads prompts and S3 creds, Maria sends contract and security docs, schedule signoff for Dec 23. Any other concerns?
[07:07] Priya Desai: Please include a simple CI test harness we can run locally to validate the run script before you start the 48h soak.
[07:14] Arjun Patel: We'll add a small smoke-suite with 50 prompts that runs in <10 minutes. We'll commit it to the shared folder.
[07:21] Lena Ortiz: Perfect.
[07:23] Maria Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the packet and run plan.
